text: Put the trumpet to your lips! Like an eagle the enemy sweeps down on the house of the LORD, because they have broken my covenant and rebelled against my law.

versions.text: Put the trumpet to your lips! Like a vulture he comes against the house of the LORD, because they have broken my covenant and rebelled against my law.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew נֶשֶׁר is most commonly the eagle, and the clause has no expressed subject; supplying "the enemy" makes the image clear for a listener, while "sweeps down on" conveys the swooping bird-of-prey imagery better than the bare "comes against."

text: To me they cry out, "My God, we know you—we, Israel!"
Israel has rejected what is good; an enemy will hunt him down.
They set up kings, but not from me; they appointed princes, and I knew nothing of it. With their silver and gold they made themselves idols—only to be cut off.
Your calf is rejected, Samaria! My anger burns against them. How long will they be unable to become clean?

versions.text: Your calf is rejected, Samaria! My anger burns against them. How long will they be incapable of innocence?
versions.explanation: "Incapable of innocence" is abstract and stumbles when read aloud; the Hebrew נִקָּיֹן carries the sense of being cleansed/pure, which reads more naturally as "unable to become clean."

text: For it came from Israel; a craftsman made it, and it is no god at all. The calf of Samaria will be broken to splinters.
For they sow the wind, and they reap the whirlwind. He has no standing grain; the sprout yields no flour. And if it should yield, strangers would swallow it down.

versions.text: They sow the wind and reap the whirlwind. The standing grain has no heads; it yields no flour. And if it did, strangers would swallow it down.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew says "standing grain he has none" — the crop itself is absent, not lacking heads. The current rendering introduces "heads," which is not in the text, and reverses the clause's subject.

versions.text: They sow the wind and reap the whirlwind. There is no standing grain for them; the sprout yields no flour. And if it did, strangers would swallow it down.
versions.explanation: The opening כִּי links this verse to the judgment announced before it and is currently dropped; also the Hebrew suffix in אֵין־לוֹ is singular ("he has none"), matching the collective Ephraim/Israel, while "for them" flattens the shift. Rendering אוּלַי יַעֲשֶׂה as "if it should yield" also reads more smoothly aloud than the clipped "and if it did."

text: Israel is swallowed up. Now they are among the nations like a vessel no one wants.

versions.text: Israel is swallowed up. Now they are among the nations like a pot no one wants.
versions.explanation: כְּלִי is a general term for a vessel or utensil; "pot" narrows the image unnecessarily, and "vessel" carries the sense of a discarded, useless object more naturally.

text: For they have gone up to Assyria—a wild donkey wandering off alone. Ephraim has bargained for lovers.
Though they bargain among the nations, I will now gather them in, and in a little while they will writhe under the burden of the king of princes.

versions.text: Though they bargain among the nations, I will now gather them in, and soon they will writhe under the burden of the king of princes.
versions.explanation: מְעָט is quantitative ("a little") rather than simply "soon"; "in a little while" preserves the Hebrew nuance and keeps the line's oral rhythm.

text: Ephraim has multiplied altars for sinning, and those altars have become his sinning.

versions.text: Because Ephraim has multiplied altars for sinning, they have become altars for sinning to him.
versions.explanation: The tail of the verse ("altars for sinning to him") is awkward for oral reading and blurs the Hebrew's deliberate echo; recasting keeps the repetition while flowing better.

text: Though I write out for him the countless precepts of my law, they are treated as something foreign.

versions.text: Though I write out for him my law ten thousand times over, it is treated as something foreign.
versions.explanation: רֻבֵּי תּוֹרָתִי refers to the many precepts/parts of the law, not to writing it repeatedly; also נֶחְשָׁבוּ is plural, matching the many precepts, so "it is treated" should be "they are treated."

text: They offer sacrifices as gifts to me and eat the meat, but the LORD takes no pleasure in them. Now he will remember their guilt and call their sins to account; they will return to Egypt.
Israel has forgotten his Maker and built palaces, and Judah has multiplied fortified cities. But I will send fire upon his cities, and it will devour her citadels.

versions.text: Israel has forgotten his Maker and built palaces, and Judah has multiplied fortified cities. But I will send fire upon his cities, and it will devour their strongholds.
versions.explanation: The pronoun shifts from "his cities" to "their strongholds" without a clear antecedent; the Hebrew suffix is singular feminine ("her citadels"), keeping the reference to the city/nation consistent.
